title: Calculation & Determinants of PED
page_title: Calculation & Determinants of PED | Cambridge (CIE) IGCSE Economics Revision Notes 2025

blocks.name: Introducing price elasticity of demand
blocks.definition: Definition of PED; Calculation of PED

blocks.md:
- The **law of demand** states that when there is an increase in price, there will be a fall in quantity demanded

  - Economists are interested **by how much** the **quantity demanded will fall**

- **Price elasticity of demand reveals how responsive the change in quantity demanded is to a change in price**

  - The responsiveness is different for different types of products
- **PED can be calculated** using the following formula:
$\text{PED = } \frac{\% \text{change} \text{in} \text{quantity} demanded}{\% \text{change} \text{in} price} = \frac{\% \Delta \text{in} QD}{\% \Delta \text{in} \mathrm{P} }$
- **To calculate a % change**, use the following formula:
$\% \text{Change} = \frac{new \text{value} - \text{old} value}{old value} \times 100$

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
A firm **raises** the price of one of its products from £10 to £15. Its **sales fall** from 100 to 40 units per day. Calculate the **PED** of this product

**Step 1:  Calculate the % change in QD**

**  **$\% \Delta \text{QD} = \frac{40 - 100}{100} \times 100

\% \Delta \text{QD} = - 60 \%$** ****(1 mark)**

**Step 2: Calculate the % change in P**

$\% \Delta \mathrm{P} = \frac{15 - 10}{10} \mathrm{x} 100

\% \Delta \mathrm{P} = 50 \%$ **(1 mark)**

**Step 3: Insert the above values in the PED formula**

$\text{PED} = \frac{\% \Delta \text{in} QD}{\% \Delta \text{in} \mathrm{P} } 

\text{PED} = \frac{- 60}{ 50} 

\text{PED} = - 1.2$ **(2 marks)**

> *The PED value will **always be negative** so economists will often **ignore the sign** and present the answer as 1.2*

blocks.name: Drawing and interpreting PED values
blocks.definition:
"Drawing and interpreting PED values:
perfectly inelastic, inelastic, unitary, elastic, 
perfectly elastic; Drawing and interpreting demand curve diagrams to show different PED"

blocks.md: - The results of the price elasticity of demand calculation tell us **how responsive consumers are to a change in price**

- The value of PED: ** 1 → ∞**
- The percentage change in quantity demanded is **more than proportional** to the percentage change in price

blocks.alt: Graph illustrating demand curve; price (£) on vertical axis, quantity demanded on horizontal. Demand decreases from P1 to P2 as quantity increases from Q1 to Q2.
blocks.caption: Consumers are very responsive to price changes

blocks.md:
- Consumers are **very responsive** to price changes

  - For example, a small price cut on airline tickets in Malaysia can lead to a large rise in bookings

- The value of PED: ** 0 → 1**
- The percentage change in quantity demanded is **less than** proportional to the percentage change in price

blocks.alt: Graph showing a downward-sloping demand curve. Price (P) increases from P1 to P2, with quantity demanded decreasing from Q1 to Q2 as price rises.
blocks.caption: Price inelastic demand

blocks.md:
- Consumers are relatively unresponsive to price changes

  - They may consider the product to be a **necessity**
- For example, cigarette sales in Indonesia fall only slightly when prices rise – demand is inelastic

- The value of PED: ** ∞**
- The quantity demanded will **fall to zero** with any percentage change in price (highly theoretical elasticity)

blocks.alt: Horizontal demand curve on a graph, price (£) on vertical axis, quantity demanded on horizontal axis, indicating perfectly elastic demand at price Pe.
blocks.caption: Perfectly elastic demand

blocks.md:
- Buyers will only purchase at **one price**, and any change causes demand to drop to zero
- For example, on global stock markets, traders may **only buy a share at a specific price**, not higher

- The value of PED: ** 0**
- The quantity demanded is **completely unresponsive** to a change in price (very theoretical value)

blocks.alt: Graph showing inelastic demand with a vertical demand line at Qe, price levels P1 and P2, and axis labels for price (£) and quantity demanded.
blocks.caption: Consumers are entirely unresponsive to a change in price

blocks.md: - For example, a patient needing life-saving insulin in India will buy it regardless of price

- The value of PED: ** 1**
- The percentage change in quantity demanded is **exactly equal** to the percentage change in price

blocks.alt: Demand curve graph showing price on the y-axis and quantity demanded on the x-axis, illustrating points P1, P2, Q1, and Q2.
blocks.caption: Consumer respond proportionally to any price changes

blocks.md: - A 5% rise in the price of a basic mobile plan in Egypt causes a 5% drop in subscriptions

blocks.name: The determinants of PED
blocks.definition: main influences on whether demand is elastic or inelastic

blocks.md:
- Some products are more responsive to **changes in prices** than other products
- The factors that determine responsiveness are called the **determinants of PED** and include

blocks.alt: Diagram illustrating the SPLAT acronym: Substitutes, Proportion of income, Luxury, Addictiveness, Time, each with corresponding icons.
blocks.caption: SPLAT - An acronym to help recall the determinants of PED

blocks.md: - Good availability of substitutes results in a **higher value of PED** (relatively elastic)

blocks.text: P – Price of product as a proportion of income

blocks.md:
- The lower the proportion of income the price represents, the** lower the PED value will be**
- Consumers are less responsive to price changes on cheap products (relatively inelastic)
- Luxury goods are more elastic because they are not essential, while necessities are more inelastic because consumers have no choice but to buy them.
- Addictiveness turns products into necessities, resulting in a **low value of PED** (relatively inelastic)

- In the short term, consumers are less responsive to price increases, resulting in a **low value of PED **(relatively inelastic)
- Over a longer period of time, consumers may feel the price increase more and will then look for substitutes, resulting in a **higher value of PED** (relatively elastic)
